subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 58-year-old man is evaluated for worsening dyspnea. Decades ago he was treated incompletely for syphilis. Blood pressure is 150/50 mm Hg with a widened pulse pressure. A high-pitched, blowing, early diastolic decrescendo murmur is heard along the left sternal border. Chest CT shows a dilated ascending aorta with calcification of the aortic root and thoracic aorta.
question: Which of the following mechanisms most likely explains the aortic dilation and calcification in this patient?

options.text: Atherosclerotic plaque rupture with medial degeneration below the renal arteries
Endarteritis obliterans of the vasa vasorum with consequent atrophy of the aortic wall
Granulomatous inflammation of the aortic media with giant cell infiltrates
Cystic medial degeneration from a fibrillin-1 mutation
Autoimmune destruction of the aortic elastic lamina by anti–smooth muscle antibodies

explanation_correct: Tertiary syphilis disrupts the vasa vasorum of the aorta (endarteritis obliterans), with consequent atrophy of the vessel wall and dilation of the aorta and valve ring. This produces calcification of the aortic root, ascending aortic arch, and thoracic aorta, and leads to aneurysm of the ascending aorta or arch and aortic insufficiency — explaining this patient's widened pulse pressure and early diastolic decrescendo murmur.

explanation_incorrect.A: Atherosclerotic abdominal aortic aneurysms classically occur below the renal arteries and involve plaque-related medial degeneration; this patient's calcification involves the aortic root and ascending arch, the syphilitic distribution.
explanation_incorrect.C: Granulomatous inflammation with giant cells in the aortic media describes giant cell (Takayasu) arteritis, a different disease that affects large elastic arteries and would show inflammatory infiltrates, not vasa vasorum endarteritis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Cystic medial degeneration from fibrillin-1 mutation is the mechanism of aortic root dilation in Marfan syndrome, a genetic disorder, and is not associated with calcification of the aortic root or a history of syphilis.
explanation_incorrect.E: There is no anti–smooth muscle antibody–mediated aortic disease in syphilis; the injury is obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum caused by the spirochete itself.

educationalObjective: Tertiary syphilis disrupts the vasa vasorum of the aorta, causing vessel wall atrophy with dilation of the aorta and valve ring, calcification of the ascending aorta, and aortic insufficiency.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 65-year-old man with a history of untreated syphilis decades ago presents with dyspnea and orthopnea. Examination shows a wide pulse pressure with bounding water-hammer pulses and a blowing early diastolic murmur along the left sternal border. Imaging shows an aneurysm of the ascending aorta with calcification of the aortic root. The pupils are small and irregular, do not react to light, but constrict on accommodation.
question: On examination of this patient's aorta, which of the following findings is most likely?

options.text: Marked narrowing of the origins of the aortic arch branches with wall thickening
A fusiform abdominal aortic aneurysm located below the renal arteries
A transverse intimal tear in the ascending aorta with surrounding hematoma
A wrinkled, corrugated intimal surface classically described as "tree bark"
Chalky white caseous necrosis of the aortic media with granulomas

explanation_correct: Syphilitic aortitis of tertiary syphilis produces calcification of the aortic root, ascending aortic arch, and thoracic aorta with a grossly wrinkled, corrugated intimal surface classically described as "tree bark." The patient also shows the two classic complications — aneurysm of the ascending aorta/arch and aortic insufficiency (water-hammer pulses, early diastolic murmur, widened pulse pressure) — plus Argyll Robertson pupils (accommodate but do not react to light), confirming neurosyphilis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Marked narrowing of arch branch origins with wall thickening describes Takayasu arteritis ("pulseless disease"), which affects the aortic arch and its branches in young women, not syphilitic aortitis.
explanation_incorrect.B: Fusiform aneurysms below the renal arteries are atherosclerotic abdominal aortic aneurysms; syphilis characteristically involves the ascending aorta and arch.
explanation_incorrect.C: A transverse intimal tear with surrounding hematoma is a Stanford type A aortic dissection, which presents with tearing chest pain and pulse deficits, not the chronic insufficiency picture of syphilitic aortitis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Caseous necrosis with granulomas is tuberculosis; pericardial involvement by TB causes constrictive pericarditis, but it does not produce a "tree bark" aorta — that is the gross signature of syphilitic aortitis.

educationalObjective: Syphilitic aortitis gives the aorta a "tree bark" appearance with calcification of the root and ascending arch, and leads to ascending aortic aneurysm and aortic insufficiency.
